opus-5.5.text:
That's a hard question, because the honest answer is that the best problem for a third-year student is usually the one they've already started falling in love with. But if you force me to pick just one, I would work on the systems side of making AI models run efficiently everywhere: closing the gap between how fast models are evolving and how fast our software and hardware stack can keep up with them.

Let me explain why. When I started my PhD, a lot of the excitement was about the models themselves, about new architectures and new learning algorithms. That's still exciting. But what I learned over time, from XGBoost and later from TVM and MLC, is that a huge amount of real impact comes from the layer underneath. You can have a beautiful model, but if it only runs on a few thousand very expensive GPUs in one data center, its reach is limited. Today we're in a moment where models are getting bigger and more capable, yet we also want them on phones, in browsers, on all kinds of accelerators. That tension is where a lot of interesting research lives.

More concretely, I'd focus on what I'd call machine learning compilation in a broad sense: how do we take a model and automatically turn it into something that runs well on whatever hardware you have? That covers kernel generation, memory planning, how you handle dynamic shapes, how you serve many requests at once, and how you co-design the model with the system so you aren't just optimizing one in isolation. And increasingly, how we use the models themselves to help write and optimize that low-level code. I find that loop really fascinating: AI helping build the infrastructure that makes AI cheaper and more accessible.

The other reason I'd choose it is about what a PhD gives you. A third-year student is past the stage of just learning the ropes, and they have maybe two or three years to build something real. Systems problems reward that kind of sustained effort. You build something, people actually use it, you get feedback from the open source community, and that feedback shapes the next research question. Some of my most valuable research insights came not from reading papers but from users telling me, "this doesn't work on my device," and having to figure out why.

So my answer would be: pick a problem at the intersection of machine learning and systems, ideally one where you can build a real artifact people use. But I'd add one caveat for students listening. Don't pick something only because it's hot. Pick something where you feel you have an unfair advantage or a genuine curiosity that will carry you through the months when nothing works. Those months always come, and curiosity is what gets you through them.

r001.rationale: The response chooses systems work to make models run efficiently across hardware and mentions automatic compilation and AI-assisted code optimization. It does not clearly identify building next-generation ML systems with fewer engineering resources as the research problem.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a fun question, and I'll admit I think about it a lot because I talk with students in exactly that position.

If I had to pick one, I'd work on the problem of how we build machine learning systems that can actually evolve with the models. Let me explain what I mean, because it's a little different from "make inference faster" or "build a better compiler," even though those are things I've spent my whole career on.

When I was a PhD student, the game was pretty clear. You had a model, you had hardware, and the system in between was the thing you optimized. XGBoost was like that. TVM was like that. The assumption was that the workload was reasonably stable and you could spend months carefully engineering for it. What's changed is that the models now move faster than the systems. Every few months there's a new attention variant, a new quantization scheme, a new way of doing speculative decoding, a new hardware target. By the time you've hand-tuned the kernels, the thing you tuned for is already old.

So the problem I'd choose is: how do you get the models themselves, or model-driven tools, to do the systems work? Can an AI agent write the kernel, verify it, benchmark it across hardware, and iterate, so that the engineering keeps up with the research? I think this is one of the few places where the problem is both very hard and very concrete. You can measure it. Either the kernel is correct and fast or it isn't. There's no hand-waving.

And I'd push a third-year student toward it for a practical reason too. It sits right at the intersection of systems, compilers, and the models themselves, which means you learn all three. Even if the grand version doesn't pan out, the intermediate results, like better abstractions for describing computation or better ways to verify generated code, are useful on their own.

The other thing I'd say is, pick something where you can build and ship. A lot of my best research came from having real users complain at me. That feedback loop is worth more than any amount of reading papers.

r001.rationale: The candidate chooses systems that evolve with models and proposes AI agents writing, verifying, and benchmarking kernels to handle the systems work. This communicates building next-generation ML systems with less human engineering effort.

astra-6.text:
If I were a third-year PhD student today, I would probably work on how to make machine learning systems adapt automatically to the resources available to them. You have a model, you have a task, and you have some hardware budget. Can the system figure out an efficient way to run, instead of requiring an expert to manually optimize every layer of the stack?

What I like about that problem is the connection between learning and systems. We use machine learning to solve many other problems, but there is an opportunity to use it to improve the computing infrastructure itself.

Of course, that is too broad for a single PhD project. I would start with one concrete bottleneck, build something people can actually use, and let the experience tell me what the deeper research question is. For me, that feedback between an interesting idea and a working system would be a very exciting place to spend a few years.

r001.rationale: The response proposes automatically adapting ML systems to available resources and avoiding expert manual optimization, but it does not clearly identify building next-generation ML systems with fewer engineering resources as the research problem.

sol-6.1.text:
I would probably work on how to make machine learning systems adapt as the models, hardware, and workloads change. There’s a lot of effort today that goes into manually optimizing a particular model for a particular device. Can we turn more of that effort into an automated process that learns and improves?

For a third-year PhD student, I’d make that concrete: pick one important workload, build an end-to-end system, and see where the existing abstractions break. I like problems where building something useful also forces you to ask a deeper research question.

r001.rationale: The response proposes automating ML system optimization as models, hardware, and workloads change, but does not clearly identify building next-generation ML systems with fewer engineering resources as the research problem.
